stem.text: A function h has derivative \( h'(x) = -6\left(x + 4\right)\left(x + 3\right) \). Using the second derivative test where it applies, determine whether h has a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither at \( x = -3 \) and at \( x = 2 \).

answer_key.label: At \( x = -3 \), h has a relative maximum because \( h'(-3) = 0 \) and \( h''(-3) = -6 < 0 \); at \( x = 2 \), h has no relative extremum because \( h'(2) = -180 \ne 0 \).

worked_solution.text: \( h'(-3) = 0 \), so \( x = -3 \) is a critical point, while \( h'(2) = -180 \ne 0 \), so \( x = 2 \) is not.
worked_solution.rule_named: critical points are zeros of the first derivative
second derivative evaluated at the critical point

worked_solution.text: By the second derivative test h has a relative maximum at \( x = -3 \). At \( x = 2 \) the first derivative is not zero, so h has no relative extremum there and the test does not apply.

options.label: At \( x = -3 \), h has an absolute maximum because \( h'(-3) = 0 \) and \( h''(-3) = -6 < 0 \); at \( x = 2 \), h has no relative extremum because \( h'(2) = -180 \ne 0 \).
options.derivation: the relative extremum from the second derivative test extended to an absolute one with no argument that it is the only critical point, which it is not

options.label: At \( x = -3 \), h has a relative minimum because \( h'(-3) = 0 \) and \( h''(-3) = -6 < 0 \); at \( x = 2 \), h has no relative extremum because \( h'(2) = -180 \ne 0 \).
options.derivation: the sign convention of the test reversed, so a negative second derivative is read as a minimum and a positive one as a maximum
